title: Joint forest management in regions dominated by highly fragmented family forestry: a tool for increasing the resilience to wildfires of forests and forest owners
content:
Abstract
Forest management is vital for climate change mitigation and increasing forest resilience to shifting disturbance regimes. In fire-prone regions, landscape-scale planning is essential but challenging, especially where land is fragmented into a large number of smallholdings. Joint Forest Management (JFM) offers a potential solution, though often forest owners are reluctant to jointly manage forests. This study assesses whether JFM can improve the resilience of forests and forest owners to wildfires in a fire-prone region in northwestern Spain without compromising other climate-related policy goals. Using simulations over a 120-year period—including historical wildfire data—we compared business-as-usual (BAU) and JFM scenarios under three climate conditions: historical, Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) 4.5, and RCP 8.5. JFM consistently reduced wildfire impact, with burned area 65 per cent higher under BAU across all scenarios. JFM also provided an additional cumulative economic benefit, of ~€18–28 million relative to BAU at year 120, depending on the climate and wildfire scenario. Additionally, JFM supported multiple strategic political goals including not only enhanced wildfire prevention but providing also enhanced wood value along the wood supply chain, and an increased total area of protected forests due to larger patches of native broadleaved forests. Our results suggest that an effort should be made by political agents to support JFM, especially during the implementation phase to overcome owners’ reluctancy.
